rv.q: Alan Strachan’s cleverly orchestrated revival of his second big hit, first seen in Scarborough in 1969, reminds us just what a comic master Ayckbourn is.
Even so, the performances are an across-the-board triumph, and if half the new plays hitting our stages at the moment were half as accomplished, what a wonderful world this would be.

But while it looks like standard sitcom fare, even in this – only Ayckbourn’s second West End hit – the playwright is already making the kind of bold and daring experiments in theatrical form that would become an artistic signature. In this case, the three men all work for the same company, and one of them is having an affair with another’s wife.
This is a triumphant return of an outstanding farce: vintage Ayckbourn, classic production.

cn.t: Critics warmly embrace this Ayckbourn revival, praising its technical ingenuity and sharp class commentary that feels remarkably undated. Strachan's direction draws strong notices, with the overlapping dual-household conceit landing as both hilarious and perceptive.
